Results, protests and appeals

Tip: It starts with the score: in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ check your card when you leave each stand, and in Compak® Sporting sign the sheet after each round. How to read it: How to read a scoreboard and results.

A protest must be made on the spot. Raise a hand and say “Protest!” or “Appeal!” while you are still on the stand. In Sporting™ do it before you call for the next target (ask for it to be thrown, for example “pull”): once you call, you have accepted the previous ruling. In Compak® Sporting do it before the next shooter calls. The referee stops the shooting and listens to your reason.

If the referee is sure, the decision stands and is final. If in doubt, the referee may ask another referee, the trapper (the person who releases the targets) or the shooters of the squad, for advice only, and then decides alone. You may not walk off the stand or go and pick up a target to check it. In Sporting™ you must break targets where the referee can see them. If the referee rules that a target was broken behind a bush, a tree or another natural obstacle, or beyond the shooting limit, that ruling cannot be appealed. The shooting limit is a line past which hits do not count.

Some decisions cannot be taken to the jury at all. In Sporting™ these are “one or zero” (hit or miss), a No Bird call (the target is thrown again), and whether the target flew correctly. In Compak® Sporting they are hit or miss, a defective target (a broken or faulty one), and a target that flew off its set path. Any other decision of the referee can be appealed to the jury in writing, with a deposit (money you leave with the appeal). In Sporting™ the deposit is 40% of the entry fee. In Compak® Sporting it is the amount that applies on the day of the competition, and you can appeal only about something that happened that same day. If the jury agrees with you, you get the deposit back.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

The jury may tell the referee to change the ruling, appoint another referee or change the ruling itself.

Compak® Sporting

The jury may instruct the referee for future decisions or appoint another referee.

International events may also have an appeal jury: a second panel you can turn to if you disagree with a decision of the jury itself. In Compak® Sporting one is set up at each international competition. In Sporting™ it is optional; where there is none, the jury’s decisions are final.

After the final ruling you must carry on shooting within fifteen seconds in Sporting™ and ten in Compak® Sporting. If you do not, it counts as a refusal to comply (not obeying the referee), which is punished. Arguing on, making a show of disagreeing, or other people openly criticising the ruling counts as an attempt to influence the referee, and that is punished too.

So protest calmly and politely. For a refusal to comply or an attempt to influence the referee, the jury can take away a target or a whole round, or exclude the shooter from the competition. Cards and penalties: Warnings, cards and penalties.

Tip: Before you protest, take a breath and be clear about what you saw. Once the ruling is final, let it go and return to your routine for the next target: Reset after a miss.

Key points

  • Protest immediately, on the stand, hand raised: “Protest!” / “Appeal!”
  • Protest before your next call: calling accepts the ruling (Compak® Sporting: before the next shooter calls)
  • Not for the jury: one/zero (hit or miss), No Bird, trajectory (Compak® Sporting: hit or miss, defective or off-trajectory target)
  • Written appeal to the jury with a deposit (Sporting™: 40% of the entry fee)
  • Resume within 15 s (Sporting™) or 10 s (Compak® Sporting); further arguing = an attempt to influence the referee

Did you know?

In Sporting™ a deposit from a rejected appeal does not vanish: it goes to a charity chosen by the FITASC Chairman.

Stand Talk

  • Shooter Protest! The target was broken before I fired.

    Meaning: The shooter formally challenges the ruling and gives the reason (here: a broken target was thrown).

  • Referee I’m certain — the decision stands.

    Meaning: The referee confirms; the ruling is final.

  • Referee Did anyone see a piece come off?

    Meaning: The referee is in doubt and asks the squad for advice only; the referee still decides.

  • Referee You can take it to the jury in writing, with the deposit.

    Meaning: This decision is appealable; a written appeal and a deposit are needed.

  • Referee Please carry on shooting.

    Meaning: The ruling is final; resume now or it becomes a refusal to comply.

For the interpreter
  • Keep “protest” and “appeal” as the formal words of the rules. Be fast here: the protest has to come before the next call. Pass on the referee’s answer at once and in full, without your own view of it. Your job is to translate the protest and the answer accurately, not to argue the case.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How do you protest correctly?

    1. After the round, at the competition office
    2. Call the next target, then explain why
    3. At once on the stand: hand up, say “protest”
    Answer

    At once on the stand: hand up, say “protest”

    A protest is made immediately on the stand; in Sporting™ calling the next target means accepting the previous ruling.

    Chapter 9 · How to protest on the stand

  2. Which decision cannot be appealed to the jury?

    1. A penalty for being late
    2. Whether a target was one or zero
    3. A warning about your dress
    Answer

    Whether a target was one or zero

    Hit or miss is decided by the stand referee alone, in both disciplines. Other referee decisions can go to the jury in writing.

    Chapter 9 · What can go to the jury and the 40% deposit

  3. In Sporting™, how big is the deposit for a written appeal to the jury?

    1. 40% of the entry fee
    2. The full entry fee
    3. A fixed 50 euros
    4. No deposit is needed
    Answer

    40% of the entry fee

    The Sporting™ rules set the deposit at 40% of the entry fee; it is returned if the jury agrees with the shooter.

    Chapter 9 · What can go to the jury and the 40% deposit
